data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive 'critical preference' grounded in risk minimization rather than probability maximization; accepting this costs us the intuitive assurance that the future will resemble the past, forcing us to act on the best-unchallenged error-elimination strategy while acknowledging it may still fail catastrophically.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference for the better-corroborated theory implicitly assumes that past test survival predicts future performance, then it smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory requires assigning it a higher subjective probability of success for practical purposes, then the distinction between corroboration and probability collapses in practice.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's formal attempt to define verisimilitude (truth-likeness) failed logically, then using 'closeness to truth' as a justification for action lacks a coherent foundation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Reframe the choice between theories not as an inference to truth or probability (which requires induction) but as a decision-theoretic rule to minimize known falsity. Since all universal laws are unproven, the rational agent selects the theory that has withstood the most severe tests (highest content + survival) because it is the only one where specific errors have been actively eliminated, whereas preferring a less-tested theory retains known potential errors without compensation. This avoids induction by refusing to claim the successful theory is 'more likely true,' claiming only that it is the 'least obviously false' option currently available.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
